newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty gains as mood bullish after losses.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty gains as mood bullish after losses.

text.p: The Polish zloty recaptured more lost ground on Wednesday, strengthening against the basket for the fourth straight trading day after a steep fall as foreign and domestic players lengthened zloty positions, dealers said.
Dealers said that small sums moved the shallow market and that foreign investors actively bought zlotys on Wednesday.

"Overall foreign capital flew into Poland today, which bodes well for the zloty in the near-term. Some say the zloty may even rise to around parity levels," said Mateusz Bieniek, dealer at Societe Generale in Warsaw.
However, others said the zloty stood to loose some ground.

"The potential for further zloty gains is not large because Poland has a widening trade deficit...and the economy has been hit by heavy floods," said Leszek Szafranek from Bank Slaski SA. "The zloty may soon return to three percent below parity."
The zloty closed at -1.09/-1.20 percent from parity, up from Tuesday's -1.90/-2.02. On Friday it was at -3.29 percent.
It closed at 3.4360/80 to the dollar, against 3.4536/65 on Tuesday and at 1.8770/05 to the mark, against 1.9010/40.
Dealers said the zloty received an additional boost by the IMF's favourable assessment of Poland's fundementals despite losses from floods in southern Poland over the last two weeks.

"Although the present level of the current account deficit (4-5 percent of GDP in 1997) is not a problem, a further significant deterioration would make Poland vulnerable to sudden shifts in confidence and resulting economic and financial disruptions," the International Monetary Fund said.

The IMF also said the recent zloty fall created room for an interest rate rise, needed to contain credit growth, and that large zloty swings within the currency's present 14-percent trading band should limit hot capital flow pressures.
On Wednesday the central bank rejected all bids at its reverse repo tender, but pushed up yields on its 91-day bills.
Some dealers said that today's rejection of all reverse repo bids may have been a signal that the central bank was in no hurry to increase nominal rates, now at 22 and 25 percent.

"The central bank will not increase rates during the summer months, but perhaps around the autumn," said Piotr Schmidt, dealer at Pekao SA. Last week the central banker said there was a very real possibility on an official interest rate rise.

Overnight rates closed at 22.60/23.10 percent, against 23.55/23.65 at opening and tomorrow/next were at 22.70/23.20 against Tuesday's 23.65/24.05. The 91-day NBP-bill yield rose 0.08 to 22.58 percent. -- Wojciech Moskwa +48 22 653 9700
